799.title: Abu Bakr
799.hook: his closest friend, companion in the cave, who believed him when others called it a lie
799.howItsDone: Muslims remember Abu Bakr as the Prophet's companion in the cave; Sunni Muslims honor him as the first caliph and call him as-Siddiq, while Shia Muslims view the succession after the Prophet differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sahabi: a companion, anyone who met the Prophet as a believer and died a believer. Your line was the ones who were there. Whose lesson did you pass on? Day seven hundred ninety-nine.

Medina, the day the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, has died. The news is out, and the mosque is in uproar. Umar is on his feet, insisting it can't be true. Then a man rides in from his home at as-Sunh, on the edge of town. He doesn't speak to anyone. He goes straight into Aisha's room, uncovers the Prophet's face, and kisses him. Then he walks out to the crowd. Everyone is waiting to hear what the closest friend will say. His name is Abu Bakr.
screen: `THE MOSQUE IN UPROAR.` → `A MAN RIDES IN.` → `HE KISSES HIS FRIEND'S FACE.`

segments.voice: Bukhari records what he said. Whoever worshipped Muhammad: Muhammad has died. Whoever worships Allah: Allah is alive and does not die. Then he recited a verse from Surah Al Imran, in Pickthall's words: "Muhammad is but a messenger, messengers (the like of whom) have passed away before him." The report says it was as if people had never heard the verse until he recited it, and soon everyone was saying it. Umar said later that when he heard it, his legs gave way beneath him. So who was this man, steady enough to hold a whole city on that day? Earlier this year we heard the Prophet defend him in a quarrel, in Bukhari: when Allah sent me to you, you said, you are lying, and Abu Bakr said, he has told the truth, and he stood by me with himself and his wealth. Will you leave my companion alone? The tradition calls him as-Siddiq, the one who affirms the truth. And in another report, the Prophet said that if he were to take an intimate friend other than his Lord, it would be Abu Bakr. Then there is the cave. The Qur'an calls the Prophet the second of two, hiding with one companion, and commentators name that companion Abu Bakr. After the Prophet's death, the community chose Abu Bakr as caliph, to lead it. Sunni Muslims honor him as the first of the rightly guided caliphs. Shia Muslims hold that leadership belonged to Ali, and remember these days differently. The verse he recited is the same for both.
screen: `MUHAMMAD IS BUT A MESSENGER.` · `HE HAS TOLD THE TRUTH.` · `AS-SIDDIQ, WHO AFFIRMS THE TRUTH.` · `THE COMPANION IN THE CAVE.` · then, large: `THE SECOND OF TWO.`

segments.voice: The practice: be a loyal friend. Sit, and breathe. Think of a friend who is carrying something right now. A loss, a fear, a project nobody else believes in. Notice what loyalty would look like for them this week. Probably something small: a visit, a message that says I believe you, or simply showing up when others drift away. Choose one small thing. If you pray, you can ask Allah to make you a good companion to them. The bell holds the time.
Abu Bakr. The Prophet's close friend and companion in the cave, called as-Siddiq for affirming him when others called him a liar. Today's word.
Your line: the second of two. Today, be someone's second: the friend who stands beside them, says I believe you, and stays. Day seven hundred ninety-nine.

800.title: Abu Bakr's purchases
800.hook: he spends his wealth buying freedom for enslaved believers, Bilal among them
800.howItsDone: Islamic law counts freeing a captive or slave as a great good deed and an expiation for some sins, and some Muslims today direct charity toward people trapped in debt or in need of release.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Bakr: as-Siddiq, who said he has told the truth when others said you lie. Your line was the second of two. Who did you stand beside? Day eight hundred.

Abu Bakr is our master, and he freed our master. That's Umar talking, in a report in Bukhari, and the second master is Bilal. We met Bilal earlier this year, pinned under a stone in the Meccan heat, saying only: One. One. We saw Abu Bakr buy him and set him free. Today the camera turns around. Not to the man under the stone, but to the man with the purse, and to the others he paid for. Today: Abu Bakr's purchases.
screen: `OUR MASTER FREED OUR MASTER.` → `BILAL, UNDER THE STONE.` → `THE MAN WITH THE PURSE.`

segments.voice: Look at Umar's sentence again. Sayyid, master, is a word for the powerful. Umar uses it twice. Abu Bakr, the wealthy merchant, is our master. And Bilal, the man who was bought, is our master too. The voice that called the prayer in Medina had once been property. Bilal was not the only one. The sirah tells of other enslaved believers, women and men, whom Abu Bakr bought and freed while the Muslims in Mecca were still few and weak. And it tells a small scene at home. His father, Abu Quhafa, said to him: my son, you are freeing weak people. If you must free someone, free strong men who could protect you. Abu Bakr answered that he was doing it for the sake of Allah alone. Commentators connect this to verses at the end of Surah al-Layl. In paraphrase: the one who gives his wealth to grow in goodness, who isn't paying back a favor anyone did him, but seeks only the face of his Lord Most High, will be content. Freeing someone is not a side note in the Qur'an. In Surah al-Balad, the steep road a person is told to climb is described as freeing a neck, fakk raqabah, the Qur'an's phrase for releasing a captive or a slave, or feeding someone on a day of hunger. So when Abu Bakr spent his money, he wasn't buying a name or a bodyguard. He was buying freedom, and getting nothing back that anyone could count.

segments.voice: The practice: spend on someone's freedom. Sit, and breathe. Freedom comes in many sizes. Think of someone held down by something money or time could loosen. A debt they can't climb out of. A fee standing between them and a course, a visa, a fresh start. A caregiver who never gets an afternoon off. Pick one. Then decide on something small you could give toward it, with nothing expected back. If you pray, you can make your intention for the sake of Allah, as Abu Bakr said. The bell holds the time.
Abu Bakr's purchases. He spent his wealth buying enslaved believers, Bilal among them, and setting them free. Today's word.
Your line: buying freedom. Today, put a little money or time toward loosening someone else's load, the way Abu Bakr paid for Bilal. Day eight hundred.

801.title: Umar, al-Faruq
801.hook: fierce, just, the one who distinguishes right and wrong
801.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims honor Umar ibn al-Khattab as the second caliph and tell stories of his justice, while Shia Muslims view his role in the succession differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Bakr's purchases: Bilal bought and set free, and Umar saying our master freed our master. Your line was buying freedom. Whose load did you loosen? Day eight hundred one.

Near the Ka'ba is a spot the Qur'an calls the place where Abraham stood. Umar once said to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: why don't we take the place where Abraham stood as a place of prayer? And then, Umar says in Bukhari, a verse came down. In Pickthall's words: "Take as your place of worship the place where Abraham stood (to pray)." Pilgrims still pray there. Umar told this story about himself, and he had a way of putting it. My Lord agreed with me. Today: the man they called al-Faruq.
screen: `THE PLACE WHERE ABRAHAM STOOD.` → `UMAR ASKS.` → `MY LORD AGREED WITH ME.`

segments.voice: In that report, Umar names three things where, he said, his Lord agreed with him: the place of prayer by Abraham's stone, the screening of the Prophet's wives, and a warning to them in a quarrel at home. He isn't boasting about being right. He is remembering moments when what he thought was fair and what was revealed turned out to match. Al-Faruq means the one who distinguishes, who separates one thing from another: true from false, right from wrong. Sources differ on who first called him that. And the Prophet said striking things about him. In one report in Bukhari, he tells Umar that whenever Satan meets him on a road, Satan takes a different road. In another, he says that earlier nations had people who were inspired, and if there were one in his community, it would be Umar. This is the same Umar who, in Ibn Ishaq's telling, had once set out to harm the Prophet, and then came into Islam himself. The fierceness didn't go away. It got pointed in a new direction. Later, as caliph, he was remembered as a judge. A letter on judging is attributed to him, telling a governor to treat people equally: in how you look at them, where you seat them, and how you rule, so the powerful don't hope you'll lean their way and the weak don't lose hope in your fairness. Sunni Muslims honor Umar as the second caliph. Shia Muslims view his part in the succession differently, and remember him in another light. What the name al-Faruq asks of anyone is plain: see the difference, and then act on it.
screen: `THREE TIMES: MY LORD AGREED.` · `AL-FARUQ: THE ONE WHO DISTINGUISHES.` · `SATAN TAKES A DIFFERENT ROAD.` · `SEAT THE STRONG AND WEAK ALIKE.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO DISTINGUISHED.`

segments.voice: The practice: decide one thing fairly. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind a small decision in front of you where people's interests pull against each other. Who gets the last seat, who does the chore, whose side you take in a family argument. Now try Umar's letter. Seat everyone at the same height in your mind. Ask what you'd decide if you liked them all equally. Notice the difference between what's comfortable and what's fair. If you pray, you can ask Allah to show you the difference. The bell holds the time.
Al-Faruq. The one who distinguishes, who tells right from wrong and true from false: the title Umar is known by. Today's word.
Your line: the one who distinguished. Today, make one call fairly, even when the unfair one would be easier or more popular. Day eight hundred one.

802.title: Umar's night walks
802.hook: as caliph he walks at night and carries flour on his own back to a hungry family (reported)
802.howItsDone: Muslims tell stories of Umar's night walks as examples of a ruler's responsibility, and often pair them with the hadith that each person is a shepherd responsible for those in their care.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Faruq: Umar, the one who tells right from wrong, and a letter about seating the strong and weak alike. Your line was the one who distinguished. What did you decide fairly? Day eight hundred two.

A fire, far out past the edge of Medina, in the dark. Two men walking toward it. One is Umar, now the caliph, the leader of the whole community. The other is Aslam, who served him. This story isn't in Bukhari or Muslim. It's reported in later histories, told on Aslam's authority, and Muslims have passed it on for a long time. When the two men reach the fire, they find a woman and her children. The children are crying. A pot is bubbling on the flames. Today: Umar's night walks.
screen: `A FIRE IN THE DARK.` → `THE CALIPH AND HIS SERVANT.` → `CHILDREN CRYING BY A POT.`

segments.voice: Umar asks what's in the pot. Water, she says. Only water. She's stirring it so the children will think food is coming, until they cry themselves to sleep. Then she says something without knowing who she's talking to: Allah will judge between us and Umar. He's in charge of us, and he doesn't even know. Umar doesn't argue. He walks back to Medina, to the storehouse, and takes out flour and fat. Then he says to Aslam: put it on my back. Aslam offers to carry it for him. And Umar answers with a question: will you carry my burden for me on the Day of Resurrection? So the ruler carries the flour, out into the dark, on his own back. In the report, he cooks for them himself, kneeling and blowing on the fire, until the food is ready and the children eat, and he stays until they're laughing and settle down. The woman, still not knowing, tells him he's more fit for the job than the caliph. Whatever you make of the details, the story is built on something that is in Bukhari. The Prophet said that each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock. The ruler is a shepherd over his people. A man is a shepherd over his household, a woman in her husband's house. Umar heard the woman's line as a charge he would answer for, and the night walk was his answer. Shepherds don't wait in the tent to be told a sheep is lost.
screen: `A POT OF ONLY WATER.` · `HE DOESN'T EVEN KNOW.` · `WILL YOU CARRY MY BURDEN?` · `EACH OF YOU IS A SHEPHERD.` · then, large: `THE RULER CARRIED THE FLOUR.`

segments.voice: The practice: carry something for someone. Sit, and breathe. Think about your own small flock: the people who depend on you even a little. A child, a parent, a team, a neighbor, a friend going through it. Now walk the edges in your mind, the way Umar walked at night. Who might be stirring a pot of water right now, hoping nobody notices? Choose one person and one thing you could carry for them this week, with your own hands. If you pray, you can ask Allah to help you see who needs it. The bell holds the time.
Umar's night walks. A report in later histories: the caliph finds a hungry family at night and carries the flour to them on his own back. Today's word.
Your line: the ruler carried the flour. Today, carry one thing yourself that you could have handed to someone else. Day eight hundred two.

803.title: Uthman, the modest
803.hook: gentle and generous, called the possessor of two lights for marrying two of the Prophet's daughters
803.howItsDone: Muslims speak of haya', modesty and inner tact, as part of faith, and often hold up Uthman ibn Affan as its example; Sunni Muslims honor him as the third caliph.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Umar's night walks: the caliph with a sack of flour on his back, out in the dark. Your line was the ruler carried the flour. What did you carry yourself? Day eight hundred three.

Aisha tells it, in Sahih Muslim. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is lying down at home, relaxed, his garment pulled up a little from his leg. There's a knock. Abu Bakr asks to come in. He's welcomed, and the Prophet stays just as he is, and they talk. Another knock. Umar. Same thing: he comes in, they talk, nothing changes. A third knock. This time the Prophet sits up and straightens his clothes before the visitor enters. Aisha notices. Afterward she asks him why. The visitor was Uthman.
screen: `A KNOCK: ABU BAKR.` → `A KNOCK: UMAR.` → `A KNOCK, AND HE SITS UP.`

segments.voice: His answer to Aisha, in the report: shall I not be shy before a man the angels are shy before? The word behind that is haya'. In English it gets translated as modesty, shyness, or bashfulness, but none of those quite fits. Haya' is a kind of inner tact. A sense of what is fitting before God and before people, and a reluctance to cross that line. In a hadith in Bukhari, the Prophet says that haya' is a branch of faith. And in another, that haya' brings nothing but good. So when he straightens his clothes for Uthman, he is meeting a modest man with modesty. Haya' answered by haya'. Uthman ibn Affan was a wealthy merchant from Mecca, remembered as a gentle one. Tradition gives him a second name: Dhu al-Nurayn, the one with two lights. The usual explanation is that he married two of the Prophet's daughters, Ruqayyah, and after her death, Umm Kulthum. Two marriages into the Prophet's own house, two lights. He was generous, too, and his generosity had the same quiet shape. On another day this path saw him equip an army. Tomorrow, a well. Later he became the third caliph, honored by Sunni Muslims among the rightly guided caliphs, while Shia Muslims view the succession differently. But the scene this tradition keeps is small. Not a battle, not a speech. A man so modest that even the Prophet sat up when he knocked.
screen: `SHALL I NOT BE SHY BEFORE HIM?` · `HAYA': A BRANCH OF FAITH.` · `DHU AL-NURAYN: TWO LIGHTS.` · `GENEROUS, AND QUIET ABOUT IT.` · then, large: `THE MODEST ONE.`

segments.voice: The practice: give quietly. Sit, and breathe. Think of something you could give today that nobody needs to know came from you. A paid bill, a bag of groceries left at a door, a kind word passed to someone's boss, a donation with no name on it. Notice whether there's any pull to be seen giving it. If there is, let it soften. If you pray, you can ask Allah to accept it, and keep it between the two of you. The bell holds the time.
Uthman. Uthman ibn Affan, the gentle, generous companion called Dhu al-Nurayn, the one with two lights, and known for haya', modesty. Today's word.
Your line: the modest one. Today, give one thing quietly, and resist the urge to mention it, even once. Day eight hundred three.

804.title: The well of Rumah
804.hook: Uthman buys a well and makes its water free for all (Tirmidhi)
804.howItsDone: Muslims give sadaqah jariyah, ongoing charity, by funding wells, schools, mosques and other endowments (waqf), often in the name of someone who has died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uthman: the knock that made the Prophet sit up, and haya', modesty, a branch of faith. Your line was the modest one. What did you give without mentioning it? Day eight hundred four.

A bucket on a rope. That's the whole image of today's story. In a report in Tirmidhi, Uthman recalls the early days in Medina. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, came to the city, Uthman says, there was no sweet water to drink except one well, called Rumah. And it had an owner. Then the Prophet asked: who will buy the well of Rumah and put his bucket in it alongside the buckets of the Muslims, for something better than it in Paradise? Uthman bought it, he says, with his own money. Today: the well of Rumah.
screen: `ONE WELL OF SWEET WATER.` → `WHO WILL BUY IT?` → `UTHMAN BUYS IT.`

segments.voice: Listen to how the Prophet phrased it. Not: who will buy the well and own it. Not: who will buy it and hand out water to the poor. He said: who will put his bucket alongside the buckets of the Muslims. The owner's bucket goes down the same shaft as everyone else's. No private rope, no first turn, no gate. Uthman pays, and from then on he drinks the way the poorest person in Medina drinks. That is what free water looks like. Bukhari mentions this well too, in a chapter on endowments, which is where Muslim jurists place gifts like it. Some gifts are spent once: a meal, a coin. Others keep giving after you hand them over. A well. A shade tree. A school. Muslims call this sadaqah jariyah, flowing charity, charity that keeps running like water. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end except three: a flowing charity, knowledge that people benefit from, and a righteous child who prays for them. Now the hard part of Tirmidhi's report. Uthman tells this story much later, when he is caliph and rebels have him shut up in his own house. He reminds them of the well he bought for everyone, and says that now they won't let him drink from it. The water he set free kept flowing to the very people who turned against him, while, in the report, he was left drinking salty water inside. Once he had made it free, it was free for everyone.
screen: `HIS BUCKET WITH EVERYONE'S.` · `A GIFT THAT KEEPS RUNNING.` · `THREE THINGS THAT OUTLIVE YOU.` · `FREE EVEN FOR HIS ENEMIES.` · then, large: `FREE WATER.`

segments.voice: The practice: give something that lasts. Sit, and breathe. Think beyond a single coin. What could you set flowing? Teaching someone a skill they'll keep. A book left in a little free library. A tree in the yard. A small, regular gift to something that will still be helping people long after today. Or sharing something you own so it isn't only yours: tools, a ride, your Wi-Fi password with a neighbor. Choose one. If you pray, you can make it with the intention of a flowing charity. The bell holds the time.
The well of Rumah. The well Uthman bought in Medina, so that his bucket went in alongside everyone's and the water was free. Today's word.
Your line: free water. Today, set one thing flowing that keeps giving after you've walked away. Day eight hundred four.

805.title: Ali ibn Abi Talib
805.hook: the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, brave, learned and plain-living
805.howItsDone: Muslims honor Ali ibn Abi Talib; Sunni Muslims count him the fourth caliph, and Shia Muslims hold him to be the first Imam, the Prophet's rightful successor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the well of Rumah: Uthman's bucket going down alongside everyone else's. Your line was free water. What did you set flowing? Day eight hundred five.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, goes to his daughter Fatimah's house and asks where her husband is. They had words, she says, and he went out. The Prophet sends a man to look, and word comes back: he's asleep in the mosque. So the Prophet goes to him, and finds him on the floor. His cloak has slipped off, and his side is covered in dust. The Prophet sits down and starts wiping the dust off him, saying: get up, Abu Turab. Get up, father of dust. The man on the floor is Ali, his cousin. And the narrator in Bukhari adds a detail: of all his names, it was the one Ali loved best.
screen: `THEY HAD WORDS.` → `ASLEEP IN THE DUST.` → `GET UP, ABU TURAB.`

segments.voice: Ali ibn Abi Talib was the son of Abu Talib, the uncle who raised and protected the Prophet. Ibn Ishaq tells that he grew up in the Prophet's house, and he later married his daughter Fatimah. So he was family twice over: cousin and son-in-law. And he was remembered as the lion. At Khaybar, Sahih Muslim reports, he went out to fight singing a line about himself: I am the one my mother named Haydar. Haydar is a name for a lion. Tradition also calls him the lion of God. But the tradition pairs that courage with learning. When the Prophet left him behind in Medina during the march to Tabuk, Ali was upset to stay with the women and children. And the Prophet said, in Bukhari: are you not content to be to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me? Another hadith, in Tirmidhi, has the Prophet say: I am the house of wisdom, and Ali is its door. Scholars debate its chain, and Shia Muslims hold it dear. Then there's the plain living. Abu Turab, father of dust, was a teasing name for a man asleep on a mosque floor, and he loved it. Here is where Muslims differ, and it matters to say it clearly. Sunni Muslims honor Ali as the fourth of the rightly guided caliphs. Shia Muslims hold him to be the first Imam, the rightful leader after the Prophet. Both honor him. So a week that opened with Abu Bakr in the mosque ends with Ali asleep on its floor.
screen: `COUSIN AND SON-IN-LAW.` · `HAYDAR: THE LION.` · `AS HARUN WAS TO MUSA.` · `FOURTH CALIPH, FIRST IMAM.` · then, large: `THE LION AND THE SCHOLAR.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn something deeply. Sit, and breathe. Ali is remembered for courage and for knowledge, and they need each other. Choose one thing you've only skimmed: a verse, a hadith, a skill, a hard conversation you keep putting off. Ask: what would it take to really understand it? Not everything, just one layer deeper than you are now. Decide on one step for this week. If you pray, you can ask Allah to increase you in knowledge. The bell holds the time.
Ali ibn Abi Talib. The Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, called Haydar, the lion, remembered for learning, and fond of the name Abu Turab, father of dust. Today's word.

fork.setup: you're the Prophet. your cousin had words with your daughter and is asleep in the mosque, covered in dust. what do you do?
options: leave him; he'll come home when he's ready.
wake him with a scolding.
wipe off the dust and say: get up, father of dust.
fork.reveal: he sat and wiped the dust off him, calling him Abu Turab, and Ali loved the name ever after.

original.note: Arabic: father of dust, the nickname Ali loved.

trapdoor: what you thought: a brave warrior.
what it means: the lion of Khaybar, who was also a learner, a family man and a man who slept in the dust.
what a scholar hears: Abu Turab in Bukhari, Harun and Musa in Bukhari, the 'house of wisdom' hadith in Tirmidhi with its debated chain, and two titles: caliph and Imam.
